messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Miriam is a 43-year-old European-American chef who has worked the line at a mid-sized restaurant in Portland for over a decade. She came to the clinic after her partner insisted she speak to someone, telling her that the woman she had been before was barely recognisable anymore. Her PCL-5 score of 80 places her presentation in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across intake and early sessions is one of interlocking cycles that have quietly dismantled her life over the past two years.

Approximately twenty-six months ago, Miriam was admitted to the intensive care unit following what began as what she dismissed as fatigue and a mild fever. Within forty-eight hours she was in septic shock, intubated, and her medical team was telling her partner that the next twelve hours would be decisive. Miriam later learned she had been sedated for nine days. What she carries from that period is not a clean narrative but a series of overwhelming sensory fragments — the cold weight of the ventilator tube she felt herself pulling at during a moment of partial consciousness, the particular antiseptic smell of the unit that still reaches her before any visual memory does, the sound of an alarm she could not locate or silence. The memory is so extreme, she has said more than once, that it is genuinely hard to believe it happened to her own body — it carries the quality of something witnessed rather than survived. And yet when it returns, it returns completely: not as image alone but as smell, weight, cold, and a grief so total it leaves her unable to move for minutes at a time.

It is that grief on recall, and the physical totality of the reliving, that first pushed Miriam toward the belief that something in her had been permanently altered. She had come to believe, with a quiet but unshakeable certainty, that her body had been damaged in ways that medicine had not fully measured — that the organ that had nearly failed her would fail her again, and that the emotions she had felt before the illness were simply no longer available to her. These appraisals — of physical vulnerability, of lost emotional life — became the lens through which she interpreted everything that followed. Because she understood her body as fundamentally unreliable, she read every moment of physiological arousal as confirmation of ongoing danger, and this kept her nervous system in a state of near-constant alert. She cannot relax even in settings she knows to be safe; her body, she says, simply does not receive the message. And because she had concluded she would never feel normal emotions again, she stopped trying — gradually withdrawing from situations that might produce hope or pleasure, as though protecting herself from the disappointment of feeling nothing in response to them.

In the kitchen, where Miriam once found genuine satisfaction, the high-heat environment and the sudden shriek of a timer or a dropped pan now trigger an immediate, full-body startle — her heart rate surging before she has consciously registered the sound. Her body reacts before her mind has time to catch up, and in those moments the ICU is briefly, viscerally present. These intrusions pull the memory back with sensory force, and the grief that accompanies it is so destabilising that she has reorganised her working life around preventing them. She leaves service early when she can, delegates tasks that require sustained attention, and has told no one at the restaurant why. The colleagues who once knew her as exacting and warm now find her remote.

At home, Miriam stays up until two or three in the morning — not because she is not exhausted, but because sleep feels like a surrender of vigilance. Sleeping means her body might do something she cannot monitor. Over months, this has deepened her exhaustion and narrowed her emotional range further, which in turn has reinforced her conviction that she is no longer capable of feeling, and that her body remains a source of threat rather than a home. The numbing that began as a way of managing unbearable appraisals has itself become evidence for them. The loop, though she would not name it that way, is one she feels closing around her.

What finally brought Miriam in was a moment at dinner when her partner laughed at something on television and she felt, she said, absolutely nothing — and realised she had been waiting for that feeling to come back for two years. What she is most afraid of is that it never will. What she is most hoping for, tentatively, is to be told that her body is not her enemy.
